title: Yunus's du'a
hook: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong (21:87)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayyub on his sickbed, and your line: you are the most merciful. Did someone ill come to mind, and did you hold them there for a moment? Today, a prophet in the dark, and a way back. Day six hundred ninety-two.

Night. Deep water. And inside a great fish, a man. The Qur'an doesn't tell us the size of the fish or how long he stayed. It tells us the prayer. The man is Yunus, the one the Bible calls Jonah, and surah twenty-one gives him a nickname: Dhu'n-Nun, the one of the fish. He had gone off in anger, the verse says, thinking he would not be hemmed in; commentators read that phrase more than one way. Now there is nowhere left to walk. So he calls out, from the darkness, in three short clauses.

Here they are, in Pickthall's translation, surah twenty-one, verse eighty-seven: "There is no God save Thee. Be Thou Glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer." Look at the order. First, there is no god but You. Before he asks for anything, he says who he is talking to. Second, glory to You, subhanak: You are above any blame. Whatever went wrong here, it didn't start with You. Third, I was wrong. The Arabic is min az-zalimin, one of the wrongdoers. Its root, z-l-m, is the root of zulm, injustice, and the classical dictionaries explain it as putting a thing where it doesn't belong. It is the same root as Adam's zalamna, four days ago. And again, notice what is missing. He doesn't blame his stubborn people, or the ship's crew who cast lots, or the fish. He doesn't even ask to be let out. The asking is folded inside the admitting. The next verse gives the answer: Allah heard him and saved him from his distress, and then the verse widens, saying that this is how He saves the believers. Surah thirty-seven adds that if Yunus had not been one who glorified Allah, he would have stayed inside the fish until the day of rising. A hadith in al-Tirmidhi calls this the du'a of Dhu'n-Nun, and says that no Muslim prays with it for anything without being answered. So Muslims who know it turn to it in tight places: a hospital corridor, a debt, a night that won't end. And Yunus says I was wrong to the One who already knew.
screen: `FIRST: THERE IS NO GOD BUT YOU.`
`THEN: GLORY TO YOU, ABOVE ANY BLAME.`
`LAST: I WAS WRONG. NO ONE ELSE BLAMED.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it three times. Sit, and let your breathing slow. If you pray, you can say the words of Yunus, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong. Three times, slowly, a breath for each part. If you don't pray, sit with the last three words alone, and let one small thing come to mind where they are true. Don't argue with it. Don't explain it. Just set it down in the dark and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Yunus's du'a. Three clauses from the belly of the fish: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong. The hadith calls it the du'a of Dhu'n-Nun. Today's word.
Your line: I was wrong. Today, say it once, out loud, to a person who is owed it, about something small and real, and add nothing after it. No but. Day six hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Some Muslims recite the du'a of Yunus, la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu min az-zalimin, in times of distress, sometimes many times over, and some gatherings recite it together when someone is in trouble.

myth: in his du'a, Yunus blames his people for his trouble
he blames no one but himself: I was wrong.
a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says this du'a is answered whenever a Muslim prays with it
it is called the du'a of Dhu'n-Nun.
the Qur'an tells us exactly how long Yunus was inside the fish
the Qur'an gives the prayer, not the length of the stay.

fork.setup: you are Yunus, in the dark inside the fish. you have one breath to call out. what do you say first?
options: there is no god but You.
my people drove me to this.
fork.reveal: he begins by naming who he's speaking to, then glorifies, then admits: I was wrong. he never even asks to be let out.

original.script: لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنْتُ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ
original.say: laa i-LAA-ha il-LAA AN-ta, sub-HAA-na-ka, in-NEE KUN-tu mi-naz-zaa-li-MEEN
original.note: Arabic: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was one of the wrongdoers (21:87).

trapdoor: what you thought: Jonah and the whale, a story for children.
what it means: three clauses in the dark: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong. the asking is folded into the admitting.
what a scholar hears: zalimin comes from z-l-m, which classical lexicons explain as putting a thing out of its proper place.

sources.quoted: There is no God save Thee. Be Thou Glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer.

notes: Pickthall wording of the end of 21:87 quoted from memory (capitalization 'God' and 'Glorified' as remembered); please confirm.

Paraphrase of 'deemed that We had no power over him' as 'sure that nothing would hold him back': commentators differ on this phrase (many read it as 'that We would not constrain him'); confirm framing.
Tirmidhi 3505 number and its wording ('no Muslim prays with it for anything without being answered') from memory; confirm number and grading.
z-l-m explained as 'putting a thing out of its proper place' follows the classical lexicons (e.g. Lane); confirm.
37:143–144 paraphrase (would have stayed until the day of rising) — confirm.

Editor review 2026-10-01: removed 'the storm' (biblical; the Qur'an has a laden ship and lots cast, 37:140–141); replaced the contested 'sure nothing would hold him back' with a hedged paraphrase; cut the superlatives 'shortest way back', 'hardest three words in any language' and 'the only One'; the word segment now uses the hadith's own name for the du'a; acknowledged the shared z-l-m root with day 688 instead of repeating its 'no one else blamed' angle as new; added Lane as the source for the z-l-m gloss.
